topic.title: Communication: Measurement and evidence in Multilingual Public Information
topic.focus: how success is evaluated and why evidence can be disputed

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-25. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Measuring the success of multilingual public-information services in the Swedish city of Malmö is harder than it looks, because the initiative was never designed with evaluation in mind. In 2015, when the city council's communications team began translating emergency notices after a public-health campaign failed to reach residents who spoke little Swedish, record-keeping was not a priority, and systematic data collection began several years later. The early period is therefore documented mainly through the recollections of professional translators, bilingual community liaison workers, and the residents who rely on translated information. These are valuable, but they cannot be checked in the way that a formal dataset can.

sections.heading: How it operates
sections.text: Current practice relies on service-uptake figures broken down by language, translation-request volumes, and complaints about missing translations. These records are produced as a by-product of a standing roster of translators and liaison workers who convert official notices into several languages before each is published, rather than by a purpose-built monitoring system. The advantage is that they cost almost nothing to collect and interrupt nobody's work. The disadvantage is that rising uptake among translated-language speakers could reflect a wider outreach campaign running at the same time rather than translation alone. Uptake rose during the same years as a separate outreach campaign, so the two effects cannot be separated. Anyone who treats these figures as precise is asking more of them than they can deliver.

sections.heading: Evidence and experience
sections.text: The strongest evidence concerns the initiative's central claim. Uptake of council services among residents whose first language is not Swedish rose by 26% between 2016 and 2023, and both the records and the impressions of those involved agree that engagement with public services has risen noticeably among residents whose first language is not English since translations became routine. The evidence on costs is much weaker. Resources devoted to a handful of widely spoken community languages leave speakers of rarer languages still effectively excluded from official information, yet that effect is rarely captured by the existing measures, so it seldom appears in any summary of performance. The difference lies in how well each side is measured, not necessarily in how much each side matters.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: A communications oversight panel that decides which languages receive priority translation has to decide how much weight to give figures that are known to be imperfect. Speakers of the twenty next most common languages, about 6% of residents, still receive nothing in their own language. The reasons behind that figure, though, are disputed. Treating the numbers as reliable can lead to decisions that later prove mistaken. Dismissing them as worthless hands the argument to whoever speaks most persuasively. Both errors have been made at different points since 2015.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: Improving the evidence would mean paying for measurement that the initiative has so far managed without, and there is a familiar objection: relying on machine translation to cover more languages more cheaply risks introducing exactly the misunderstandings that human translation was introduced to prevent. A smaller step would be to review the existing records for the specific weakness described above, namely that rising uptake among translated-language speakers could reflect a wider outreach campaign running at the same time rather than translation alone. A review of that kind could be completed within a single funding year and would at least show how far the current figures can be trusted.

The early period is therefore documented mainly through the recollections of professional translators, bilingual community liaison workers, and the residents who rely on translated information. These are valuable, but they cannot be checked in the way that a formal dataset can.

Paragraph 2 — How it operates
Current practice relies on service-uptake figures broken down by language, translation-request volumes, and complaints about missing translations. These records are produced as a by-product of a standing roster of translators and liaison workers who convert official notices into several languages before each is published, rather than by a purpose-built monitoring system. The advantage is that they cost almost nothing to collect and interrupt nobody's work. Uptake rose during the same years as a separate outreach campaign, so the two effects cannot be separated. Anyone who treats these figures as precise is asking more of them than they can deliver.

Paragraph 3 — Evidence and experience
